HEADLINE: Aussie dollar expected to reach US85¢ in 2018
TEXT:
A continued slide in the greenback could see the Aussie dollar push as high as US85¢ by the end of next year, analysts at Commonwealth Bank say.

The bullish call coincides with a fresh push in the local currency towards US80¢ on Wednesday following a much stronger than expected construction data for the June quarter. The Aussie fetched US79.9¢ in afternoon trade.

CBA's call for the Aussie to buy US85¢ by the end of 2018 is above the median economist forecast of US80¢, on Bloomberg numbers.

Weakness in the US dollar explains much of this expected strength in the local currency, CBA chief currency strategist Richard Grace said in a note to clients, as trends that were apparent in late 2016, but which were knocked off course by the shock election of Donald Trump as US President, reassert themselves.

Mr Trump's electoral victory in November had seemed a watershed moment for the world's pre-eminent currency. Analysts and investors bet the Republican-dominated Congress would give the green light to tax cuts, more spending on infrastructure and other stimulatory policies.

Correspondingly, the perception was that money flowing back into a rejuvenated American economy would push the US dollar higher in 2017.

"We had temporarily changed our US dollar depreciation view on December 9 because Trump campaigned on pro-growth policies; in particular, significantly lowering the US company tax rate," Mr Grace said.

But rather than push through legislation, Mr Trump has been busy, in turn, igniting and extinguishing various controversies that have distracted from pursuing his party's agenda.

The Bloomberg US dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, had jumped by 4.3 per cent by the end of 2016 following the election, but has since dropped 10 per cent in 2017.

Similarly, the Aussie dollar dropped around US4¢ after the US election to end 2016 at around US72¢ - only to rally 10 per cent to close to US80¢ now.

In May the CBA analysts reverted to their previous view of a weaker, rather than stronger, greenback, and have now lowered their forecasts "as the US dollar has fallen even more rapidly than we anticipated".

The factors to weigh on the US dollar are the same, Mr Grace said. Specifically, while the US Fed is poised to lift rates again by the end of the year, the monetary tightening in other jurisdictions, such as Europe, will have a "greater appreciating impact on their exchange rates" this year and the next.

Also, "fiscal policy inaction by the Trump administration, particularly in the area of cuts to the US company tax rate, will continue to work against the US dollar", Mr Grace said.

But the Aussie's strength will not be explained purely by the greenback's weakness, as "a strengthening synchronised global economy is typically bullish for Aussie and the commodity currencies", he said.

The other reason is that "a narrowing Australian current account deficit, and an improving Australian economy are currently having an even more supportive, and appreciating effect, on the dollar than we originally anticipated".

HEADLINE: Flight Centre trio defy headwinds to surpass $2b
TEXT:
Travel retailer Flight Centre keeps defying predictions of its demise, and continues to make its trio of founders extremely wealthy.

Shares in the company that Financial Review Rich Listers Graham "Skroo" Turner, Geoff Harris and Bill James established - and still own large stakes in - are up 58 per cent since January 1.

Combined, the trio hold about $2.1 billion worth of shares today - a far cry from when they made their debut on the Rich List in 1999 with total wealth of $398 million between them.

Back then, Flight Centre was a market darling but on the verge of first being written off as a victim of the first dotcom boom and the internet, where ease of purchasing flights and making hotel bookings directly for consumers was going to spell the end of the company's bricks and mortar retail model.

There have been times since when Flight Centre's share price has dipped markedly, only to recover. It went as low as $4.33 in early 2009 after the global financial crisis of the previous year but is now trading at more than 12 times that level.

Flight Centre shares have risen 34 per cent in the past 12 months, and are closing in on the company's record price of $53.75 achieved in late March 2014.

After posting five profit downgrades in three years, Flight Centre announced a $230.8 million net profit for the 2017 financial year earlier in August. The result was received well by the market, coming in at the top of the range of the company's previous guidance.

Turner remains at the helm of the company, while Harris and James have dabbled in venture capital and commercial property investments since leaving their management roles last decade.

But each maintain their large shareholdings in the firm that traces its origin back to them forming the Top Deck travel business in Britain in the 1970s. He and wife Jude also own the private Spicers Retreats luxury hotel chain, which operates rural and urban retreats in Queensland and NSW.

Harris was an early investor in the successful Boost Juice chain and now has backed Mexican food chain Fonda and the live real estate auction app Gavl.

James has published a field guide to walking the Kokoda Track in Papua New Guinea and owns commercial real estate throughout Sydney.

 How the rich invest

Graham TurnerAge: 68Sector: TravelLives: Brisbane

KEY POINTS▪ Founded Flight Centre with Geoff Harris and Bill James▪ Remains chief executive and major shareholder▪ With wife Jude owns Spicers Retreats luxury hotel chain

HEADLINE: Silvergrass mine will buff up Rio's iron ore credentials, Jacques says
TEXT:
Rio Tinto chief executive JS Jacques says the new Silvergrass mine in Western Australia will cement the miner's place as a high-margin iron ore producer and help meet Chinese demand for quality ore.

Restructuring of the Chinese steel industry has driven a wide differential between the prices for higher grade and lower grade iron ore. Steel mills prefer higher grade products to improve efficiency.

Lower grade iron ore miners including Fortescue Metals Group have insisted the bigger "discount" on their product is temporary and will slowly correct.

But Mr Jacques said Rio Tinto hoped the change, which has increased demand and pricing for its key "Pilbara Blend", was structural.

"Investing in WA like we are with Silvergrass is absolutely essential to maintain the quality of the blend for the Chinese industry," Mr Jacques said.

The dynamic is encouraging the miner to focus more on extracting higher grade ore from its Pilbara assets rather than regaining its position as a producer championing the Pilbara's lowest operating costs. Fortescue Metals Group now lays claim as the region's lowest-cost producer.

"As far as we are concerned the primary driver for us is the margins, the EBITDA margin, because at the end of the day it is all about the cash and in the context of the restructure of the steel industry, what is important is being able to provide the right product with the right grade to the right customers," Mr Jacques said.

"If you look at the last 20 years we have been making 50 to 60 per cent EBITDA margin on average. There is no doubt it [iron ore] is a fantastic business, we want to continue to invest and Silvergrass is the latest example of our approach."

Mr Jacques, Rio's iron ore chief Chris Salisbury and West Australian Premier Mark McGowan officially opened the Silvergrass mine in Western Australia's Pilbara on Wednesday.

The $US338 million ($424 million) project is Rio Tinto's 16th iron ore operation and the largest iron ore development under way in Western Australia's Pilbara region since Gina Rinehart's $10 billion Roy Hill iron ore mine, which opened in December 2015.

The 10 million tonne per annum final stage of Silvergrass is expected to commence production in the fourth quarter of 2017 and will bring the operation to a total 20 million tonnes a year.

Mr McGowan told the employees and media gathered at Silvergrass that Rio's investment in the mine was one of a few early signs the state's economy had "turned a corner" and confidence was slowly improving.

Mr Jacques said the company's position surrounding the major Grasberg copper-gold mine in Indonesia was "very clear". After years of tension, Freeport-McMoRan said it has reached an "understanding" with the government which would see it divest a further 41.64 per cent stake in the copper-gold mine but be allowed it to continue to operate it.

Rio Tinto has an interest in Grasberg through its joint venture with Freeport which entitles it to about 40 per cent of the mine's output above certain levels.

Mr Jacques said Rio had a team in Jakarta and was in "ongoing discussions with Freeport" but there was still "very little detail available".

"Grasberg is an option for us and depending on the outcome of the negotiation between Freeport and the government of Indonesia we will review our position.

"There is no doubt that Grasberg as a mine, as resource is a world-class resource. But there is a difference between having a world-class resource and a world-class business. Depending on the outcome of the negotiation then we will decide if we want to stay or if we want to go."

The reporter travelled to Silvergrass as a guest of Rio Tinto.

HEADLINE: NAB issues tougher ID, credit checks to counter identity theft
TEXT:
National Australia Bank is rolling out a new round of identification and income checks for property borrowers in response to increased security and regulatory pressures.

Borrowers, including those applying online, will have to provide photo ID and supporting documents to be verified by the mortgage broker arranging the deal. Other lenders are introducing similar policies.

Interest-only borrowers will have to answer more comprehensive questions about whether that type of loan is suitable for their needs, or if a principal and interest loan may be better.

Lenders are responding to regulatory pressure to improve scrutiny of borrowers' capacity to service loans, particularly interest-only borrowers.

Questions range from if they are borrowing as owner-occupiers or investors, through to how they can cope with temporary income reduction, or a large expense item, such as school fees or renovations.

Interest-only borrowers will also need to disclose if they will require additional bridging finance.

"It will ensure customers take out interest-only lending in the right circumstances, which is suitable for their needs," a bank memo says.

NAB is also tightening credit policies, such as verification of bonus income, and more closely scrutinising any regular deductions from PAYG income, such as superannuation salary sacrifice.

Commissions can be considered when they regularly top up a base salary, or where it is consistent and regular for a minimum of six months.

Mortgage brokers will have to provide updated photographs for all existing NAB customers who take out a new mortgage with the bank. They will also need to provide a physical or scanned copy of a certified photograph, such as a driver's licence or a passport.

The bank will also require consent forms from the borrower, any guarantors, employers and the broker.

The new verification of identity rules are in response to policies being introduced by the Australian Registers National Electronic Conveyancing Council, which is tackling online fraud.

It highlights increased awareness of identity theft, particularly for online loan applications, using stolen or forged drivers' licences, utility bills and passports.

Independent bank-sponsored agencies, such as Equifax, estimate identify theft is growing by 80 per cent a year, the fastest-growing source of fraud for banking, superannuation, credit card and insurance providers.

The tightening follows warnings by the chairman of the federal government's Black Economy Taskforce that rampant identity theft can "systemically undermine" the nation's financial and banking system.

The taskforce is expected to call for tighter controls and closer monitoring in its final report, which is expected within weeks.

HEADLINE: Metcash to clip ticket on $1b of indie sales
TEXT:
Metcash will clip the ticket on about $1 billion of stock now sourced by IGA retailers directly from suppliers as part of the wholesaler's Amazon defence strategy.

Metcash is putting the final touches on a new online portal known as indieDirect, which will enable independent retailers to link up directly with suppliers to make contact with a wider range of independent retailers.

Unveiling details of indieDirect at Metcash's annual meeting yesterday, chairman Rob Murray and head of supermarkets Steve Cain said the portal would enable independent retailers to source a wider range of products to differentiate themselves from Coles and Woolworths and better compete with Amazon.

It will also enable Metcash to play a role by negotiating better deals with suppliers on behalf of retailers and earn a small commission or margin on additional sales without having to distribute or hold the stock.

Mr Cain said most IGA retailers sourced about 70 per cent of their stock from Metcash and about 30 per cent directly from suppliers.

"There's a big opportunity for us to be involved in a larger part of that if we can negotiate better deals for them on the 30 per cent they don't buy from us," Mr Cain told the AGM. "There's a big opportunity to make a higher margin on that. That's a $1 billion business."

Mr Murray said the opportunity was unique to Metcash, as Woolworths and Coles already handled 100 per cent of the stock sent to stores.

"We intend to mind the gap, to fill that 30 per cent gap of unfilled potential," Mr Murray said.

IndieDirect is expected to be rolled out later this year.

In a recent report, Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Simotas said the new portal would migrate about $1 billion in "charge-through" sales online.

"Currently, paper catalogues are used and orders are taken by fax and phone," Mr Simotas said. "Over time, this should make the ordering experience simpler for retailers, save costs for suppliers and ... boost revenues for Metcash by providing access to some of the 5 to 10 per cent of packaged goods volume sold by retailers but not ordered through Metcash."

Metcash shareholders overwhelmingly voted to re-elect Mr Murray to the board, despite concerns about his role at Dick Smith, where he was chairman for 10 months before the electronics chain collapsed in January 2016.

Metcash also avoided a second strike against its remuneration report after making changes in response to concerns raised last year about short-term incentives paid to chief executive Ian Morrice in 2016.

Shareholders approved the grant of another 184,982 performance rights to Mr Morrice, even though he retires in December and hands the reins to CEO-elect Jeff Adams, who joins Metcash next week from Tesco's Thailand business. Mr Morrice will serve as an adviser to the company until June 2018.

Mr Murray defended the grant, saying the board wanted Mr Morrice to remain motivated during the transition period: "We're going through a CEO handover and we want both CEOs lined up on the same incentives to create long-term shareholder value," he said. "We believe if there's a good handover and good continuity the shareholders are ultimately going to win."

 Mr Morrice said sales in food and grocery in the first quarter of 2018 continued to be squeezed by competitive pressures and difficult economic conditions in Western Australia, one of Metcash's largest markets.

The headwinds were expected to continue through the year, but Metcash had plans to mitigate the impact, including cost savings from its Working Smarter program.

Hardware earnings would be boosted by a full year of earnings and synergy benefits from Home Timber & Hardware, which was acquired last October from Woolworths, while the liquor business remained well placed to grow even as market growth moderated.

HEADLINE: CBS deal values free-to-air broadcaster above $500m
TEXT:
CBS' shock bid for Network Ten, which gazumped Lachlan Murdoch and Bruce Gordon, values the free-to-air broadcaster at $500 million at least.

A report on the state of Ten's finances in administration and the sale process is expected to be given to creditors on Thursday.

The United States media giant put in a claim for $795.5 million after Ten went into administration, making it the Australian broadcaster's largest creditor.

However, in assessing the claim, the value of CBS's debt was brought down to $350 million, to reflect the fact the US studio could sell its content, which was the basis for the large majority of its claim, elsewhere.

CBS will not attempt to claim any of its debt - it is an unsecured creditor. The debt, combined with payments to secured creditors, amounts to $490 million. Other unsecured creditors will also receive payments based on an assessment on the value of their debt, and it's believed that would take Ten's valuation above $500 million.

The cash payment CBS makes for Ten is expected to be much lower than $500 million, factoring in its $350 million claim.

Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Mr Murdoch, Mr Gordon and James Packer will be paid a combined $140 million as secured creditors.

A court granted orders for administrator KordaMentha to pay out secured creditors. The date for the second meeting of creditors will be fixed in the coming days. When the secured creditors are paid out, they will not be creditors for the purpose of that meeting.

Industry observers believe at least $500 million is a truer valuation of Ten, which had a market capitalisation of $58 million when it collapsed.

One insider suggested Ten's valuation was dragged down because of the broadcaster being stuck in News Corporation's tangled web, with Mr Murdoch privately owning 7.7 per cent of shares and Foxtel, which is half-owned by News Corp, owning almost 15 per cent.

Creditors such as Cricket Australia, Endemol Shine (which is part owned by Murdoch-controlled 21st Century Fox), Fremantle Media, ITV Australia and staff are expected to be paid as part of periodic payments as CBS begins to run Ten, depending on negotiations, therefore addressing their claims.

The biggest remaining debt lies with 21st Century Fox - believed to have been valued at $200 million. The return Fox gets will depend on whether it continues to supply Ten with content. Sources said if Fox did not come to an agreement with Ten, the studio would get cents in the dollar on its contract.

When Ten was put into voluntary administration in June, directors said they negotiated draft agreements with both CBS and Fox that would reduce Ten's US content costs by 50 per cent.

The CBS deal to purchase Ten also raises questions about the free-to-air broadcaster's advertising sales. Ten's ads are sold by Multi-Channel Network, which is a joint venture of Foxtel, which is 50-50 owned by Telstra and News Corp, Fox Sports, which is wholly owned by News Corp, and Ten with 24.99 per cent.

CBS and News Corp officials have been cautious not to speculate on future moves.

MCN will begin its negotiations with advertisers next month, and the CBS deal is not expected to be finalised until October.

There is a huge amount of work in putting together a sales team for Ten, and all the systems and data needed to do so. It seems unlikely that CBS, if it were to end the MCN arrangement, would do so in the next six to 12 months.

The bid from CBS needs approval from creditors, a court and the Foreign Investment Review Board, while the Murdoch-Gordon bid relies on changes to media laws now stalled in the Senate.

CBS's bid comes as a surprise to Australia's media sector. While it had previously come to a draft agreement with Ten to cut the price of its content deal in return for equity before the network fell into administration, the US studio appeared to distance itself from buying the broadcaster.

HEADLINE: Ramsay Health boss flags new acquisitions abroad
TEXT:
Australia's largest private hospital operator Ramsay Health Care is scoping out Germany and Scandinavia as possible new beachheads for its hospitals business, with new chief executive Craig McNally declaring acquisitions are on the radar.

Mr McNally - the former chief operating officer and a 29-year company veteran - said while Australia remains the powerhouse of Ramsay's operations, posting strong earnings growth in fiscal 2017, its European businesses delivered on expectations in a tough environment, and he is keeping an eye out for acquisitions.

"We are acquisitive ... my role in the company has been around growth and strategy and I remain committed to that," Mr McNally told The Australian Financial Review.

Ramsay is reviewing possible deals in markets in which it already operates, such as Britain and France, but is also looking into new countries like Spain and Germany, and areas such as Scandinavia and Asia. Mr McNally said the US eventually could be a consideration, but not now given the political and healthcare market uncertainty.

"We are a disciplined acquirer and we do a lot of homework," said Mr McNally, who took over the top job just eight weeks ago from long-serving CEO Chris Rex.

"Scandinavia and Germany as new markets are most attractive given the dynamics and where we see certain opportunities present.

"The same fundamentals that drive other Western markets are driving Germany which has a strong health system, and the role of the private sector is critical to the success of the overall health sector.

Watermark Funds Management analyst Nick Cameron said given Ramsay's recent debt refinance and declining leverage, it could easily stomach a $1 billion deal.

"While France is likely off the table in terms of big acquisition, I would not be surprised if they do something in Europe," he said. "Ramsay is an acquisitive company and is due to make another large accretive deal."

Ramsay's last major beachhead was made in France in 2010. Since then it has invested heavily, doing a $1.2 billion deal to acquire the nation's largest private hospital operator, Generale de Sante, in 2014. The regulatory environment has not been easy; the former Hollande government issued two years of tariff cuts and Mr McNally said Thursday another cut is expected March 2018.

Mr McNally said it will be later this year before he gets any indication about the healthcare landscape under new President Emmanuel Macron, whose popularity in recent weeks has dived on the back of tough debates in French parliament over labour reform.

"There is uncertainty, while there is a view he is pro-business ... there is nothing come out from the perspective of the health sector," he said. "We need to get some clarity on tariffs before we take views on any growth."

Revenue at its French unit was virtually flat at €2.2 billion ($3.3 billion) in the 2017 financial year, and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortisation, and restructuring or rent costs (EBITDAR) also was nearly flat at €448.3 million. Mr McNally warned no growth is expected this year in France, or Britain, where revenue was up 4.6 per cent to £449.2 million ($728.3 million) while EBITDAR was up 1.7 per cent to £113.9 million. An increase in tariff in Britain is scheduled for April 2018.

Ramsay met its full year guidance, posting core net profit growth of 12.7 per cent to $542.7 million due to increasing admissions and earnings in its Australian business. The $13.8 billion company is tipping core EPS growth this new 2018 fiscal year of 8 per cent to 10 per cent, lower than its past double-digit growth expectations.

Mr McNally said guidance is still supported by strong growth in its Australian hospitals as the public system remains under pressure and admissions continue to rise due to an ageing and growing population. Ramsay has not deviated in its view of the local market, with plans to invest up to another $250 million of brownfields in 2018.

But investors were not impressed, with the stock tumbling 5.2 per cent, or $3.78, to $68.10.

"This is a classic case of diworseification," said one fund manger. "They have a cracking Aussie business in greenfields and mostly exciting brownfields. Returns are very high. But then they have gone and thrown money at France and UK, and Craig has been a driver of that strategy, so they are not about to change tack.

"They will be diluting group returns over time as France and UK grow. They need to get both France and UK humming before making a beachhead move."

Mr McNally staunchly defended Ramsay's move offshore saying these are long-term investments, and pointed to analysts' estimation that Ramsay will gain $80 million to $100 million in procurement synergies over a four-year period.

Australian hospitals (and pharmacy) revenue grew 7 per cent to $4.7 billion in the year ended June 30. Australian earnings before interest and tax climbed a strong 13.7 per cent to $649.6 million,

Mr McNally said Ramsay made some headway with its new pharmacy franchise, which is on track to total 55 retail pharmacies. He sees that growing to several hundred outlets over the next three years, and eventually would like to have clinics within the pharmacy to help deal with outpatient chronic diseases.

HEADLINE: Infrastructure boom upon us, says Boral boss
TEXT:
Boral chief executive Mike Kane expects Australia's infrastructure boom to last up to 10 years and deliver bigger profit momentum than the housing boom, which is slowly easing but will still stay well above long-term averages.

Mr Kane has reassessed his own view of the future strength of Australia's infrastructure pipeline of projects as governments spend more on roads, freeways, railway projects and bridges, and has extended his forecast for the boom period from five or six years, to seven to 10 years.

"The infrastructure boom is on us right now," he said on Wednesday, highlighting that concrete prices rose 3-5 per cent in most metropolitan markets in 2016-17, except in the weaker Western Australian economy.

Boral is also expected to generate strong demand for its concrete, cement and quarrying products from the strength in housing construction.

While housing construction markets on the eastern seaboard were off their record-breaking peaks, the tapering off was gradual, and the market remained strong.

"It's moderating, but it's moderating at a very slow rate," he said. "The housing market is nowhere near receding to anywhere near the norm."

In the United States, where Boral generates about 25 per cent of its earnings from Texas, there will be a short-term blip from the severe flooding in Houston after Hurricane Harvey.

"We have a few plants that are shuttered in the impacted area," Mr Kane said. He said it was too early to say what the short-term impact would be on profits.

But he was confident the Texan economy would recover fast after the floodwaters subsided.

Texas has been a profit powerhouse state for Boral for the past 20 years, and Mr Kane said demand would shoot up as the rebuilding occurred.

The other big global hotspot, North Korea, is also something of a dilemma for Boral, which derives 23 per cent of revenues in its USG Boral sheet rock business from the South Korean market. But Mr Kane said there had been 30 years of tensions and uncertainties, and those further from the epicentre tended to be more spooked than the locals in South Korea. "They tend to take it in stride," he said.

Boral expects 15 per cent growth in 2017-18 in the value of work the company is doing on roads, highways and bridges in Australia as governments spend on big-ticket projects.

Boral's local arm is part way through projects such as NorthConnex and Sydney Metro in NSW, and the Northern Connector freeway in South Australia.

It is also tendering for bigger projects such as the Melbourne Metro and Western Distributor in Victoria, and also has its eye on the second Sydney airport at Badgerys Creek.

Mr Kane said new housing starts were expected to fall about 12 per cent to 190,000 in 2017-18 and the renovations market was forecast to remain steady after a 3 per cent rise in 2016-17. Housing starts hit a peak of 234,000 in 2015-16. The long-term "norm" is 150,000.

On Wednesday, Boral raised its final dividend marginally to 12¢ per share from 11.5¢ per share a year ago, after announcing a 16 per cent increase in net profit after tax to $296.9 million.

Total revenue was up 1.8 per cent to $4.39 billion. Profit before tax and one-offs was up 22.3 per cent to $409.2 million. The 50 per cent franked final dividend will be paid on October 3.

Citi analyst Simon Thackray said the EBITDA margins in Australia of 16 per cent "set a new high water mark". Boral shares were 2.9 per cent lower at $6.63 at the close on Wednesday. They were fetching $6.32 a year ago.

Mr Kane is now spending about half his time in the United States as Boral integrates the $US2.6 billion Headwaters fly ash and building products operations.

Boral made a big bet on the future strength of the American economy when it announced the Headwaters acquisition in November 2016.

Boral North America, the newly-established division, which combined the Headwaters business with Boral's existing US operations, increased its earnings before interest and tax by 50 per cent to $66 million.

It included a $US21 million ($28 million) contribution from eight weeks of full ownership of the Headwaters business, which Mr Kane said was in line with the guidance provided when the purchase was announced.

Mr Kane, who has strongly criticised policymakers in the past, said he had lowered his expectations of what could be achieved in Washington and Canberra by politicians, and that way he wouldn't be disappointed.

"At the end of the day I tend to ignore the noise," he said. Instead, his focus was more on the real-world economy.

HEADLINE: Top award for HECS designer
TEXT:
Australian National University economist Bruce Chapman was honoured with The Australian Financial Review Higher Education Lifetime Achievement Award at a gala dinner for his role in designing the Higher Education Contribution Scheme (HECS), which has underpinned university funding for nearly 30 years.

In selecting Professor Chapman for the award, the judges said it was thanks to his work "that Australia has been able to expand access to higher education in an equitable and cost-effective way".

Professor Chapman said in a speech to the dinner on Tuesday night that he believed it was the introduction of HECS loans that had kept university education affordable in Australia.

"Without it, I've no doubt, we would have ended up with fees, financed with bank loans, as they do in the United States," he said. "Pernicious bank loans that can ruin the lives of student debtors because they ruin their credit reputation."

He paid tribute to then education minister John Dawkins, who was at the dinner, for backing the concept of income contingent loans - and steering it past opposition from students, a reform-weary public, crossbench senators, and his own Labor Party - to make it a reality.

"It was an example, a consummate example, of extraordinary politics," Professor Chapman said as he accepted the award, which was sponsored by UniSuper.

Other winners of other AFR Higher Education Awards were:

Emerging Leader Award, sponsored by Perrett Laver: Professor David Reilly from the University of Sydney.

Community Engagement Award, sponsored by UniSuper: Central Queensland University - Choices Applied Theatre Project.

Education Technology Award: Swinburne University of Technology - Quitch.

Employability Award, sponsored by Pearson: Macquarie University - Enhancing the Employability of Macquarie Graduates.

Equity and Opportunity Award: La Trobe and Federation University - Higher Education for Care Leavers Strategy.

Facilities Innovation Award, sponsored by Atira: RMIT - The 40-year Life-Cycle.

Industry Engagement Award, sponsored by TechnologyOne: Monash University - Monash Industry Team Initiative: MITI.

International Education Award, sponsored by Top Education: University of Adelaide - China Career Ready Plus Program.

Learning Experience Award: UTS: Hatchery

HEADLINE: STEM focus 'one of the worst things we've done'
TEXT:
Australian National University professor and former Intel researcher and anthropologist Genevieve Bell has described the focus on science, technology, engineering and maths skills as "one of the worst things we have done in the last decade".

Dr Bell, who was speaking at The Australian Financial Review Higher Education Summit, returned from Silicon Valley this year to take a position at ANU, and despite spending the bulk of her career at the epicentre of technology, she said the double down on STEM at the expense of humanities and the arts was a huge mistake.

"If you talk to most scientists, the most productive conversations they frequently have are outside of their disciplines and their fields and their biggest inspirations frequently come from the places that aren't inside their own skillset," Dr Bell said.

"You need the arts and the humanities as much as the sciences because that's how you build a nation ...We sometimes get so focused on the tyranny of STEM we forget there are all these other ways of making sense of the world that are valuable and useful, and not just because they feed STEM, but because they feed a world we all want to make happen."

Dr Bell, who is now part of the ANU's College of Engineering and Computer Science, is leading the creation of a new, as yet unnamed, applied science field centred around how humans and the world should look as data shifts to the forefront.

She believes this new applied science will be crucial to guiding the regulatory and ethical consequences of this movement towards data-driven decisions and increased autonomy of technology, so people end up living in a society they want to be part of.

Dr Bell said a major component of this was critical questioning, informed by disciplines outside technology.

"If you look at a lot of the foundational leadership from the 19th and 20th century, there is an idea that the manifestation of our humanness isn't just through scientific endeavour, it's through literature and arts and through being able to ask hard questions about who we are and how we came to be," she said.

"In some ways the most important checks on science, technology, engineering and maths come from other disciplines. They come from asking questions about is this really necessary? What are the ethical consequences of this? What is the world that is being imagined here?"

Dr Bell joined Intel in 1988 from Stanford University and spent almost two decades of her career at the technology company, becoming a vice-president and a senior fellow.

 As computers give way to data as driver of change, Dr Bell said it would soon inhabit our environments, not be confined to devices.
